content:
The last chapter, Full Stop, by the write-a-chapter procedure. It's where this memoir stops and that book doesn't.

Material:
- After the demo I didn't decide to stop working on Full Stop. I just didn't open it the next evening, or the one after. The wall stayed empty. The pin holes are still there, in pairs.
- The email in which Red quoted line six hundred and twelve back to me was the one where he asked a different question. He'd read the README twice by then. He asked: "Is there a book in here?" He meant the tool, and the three years, and me. I said I didn't know, and then I started this one, which is how I found out.
- This book was written with the tool. It read every chapter every night against what the book had promised and told me when one disagreed. It told me several times. I fixed most of them.
- Full Stop has eleven chapters. It still does. Chapter four still credits its shop, and chapter nine still credits the rival, and the footnotes still point at each other, and I've stopped minding. The shoeboxes are in a closet. The radiator card is in one of them; I'm still not sure where.
- Last week Hedda asked how the book was. I said, "Which one?" She wrote that down.

The chapter says, once, what the spec says: a tool built to avoid a book can still be how a book gets finished; it just isn't the book it was built for. It doesn't explain it, and it doesn't add a moral.

Don't end on the words "full stop". Everyone will be waiting for it, which is the best reason not to.

After the demo I didn't decide to stop working on Full Stop.
I didn't decide anything.

He meant the tool, and the three years, and me.

I said I didn't know.
Then I started this one, which is how I found out.

This book was written with the tool.
Every night it read every chapter against what the book had promised, and told me when one disagreed.

I fixed most of them.

A tool built to avoid a book can still be how a book gets finished.
It just isn't the book it was built for.

Full Stop has eleven chapters.
It still does.

The shoeboxes are in a closet.
The card from behind the radiator is in one of them.
I'm still not sure where.

Last week, in the last four minutes, Hedda turned her chair away from her monitor and asked how the book was.

"Which one?" I said.

She wrote that down.

2. Red's email that quoted line six hundred and twelve asks "Is there a book in here?", and Cy starts this one.

5. Full Stop still has eleven chapters, the footnotes still point at each other, and the radiator card is somewhere in the shoeboxes. "It still does" picks up the same line from How's the Book?
6. It closes with Hedda's question, "Which one?", and "She wrote that down."

It doesn't end on "full stop". I added two short lines of my own after the first paragraph: "The evenings went to the tool, as they had for months. Nobody noticed, including me." Cut them if they're not yours.

The chapter now also binds `people-who-ask` and `written-with-the-tool`, because it carries Red's second question, Hedda's fourth answer and the repeated admission.

**Spec changes**, each with a trail entry pointing at your message:
- **#people-who-ask** now has Red's later email ("Is there a book in here?", after reading the README twice), Cy starting this book, and "Which one?" to Hedda.
- **#not-the-book-it-was-built-for** now says the last chapter states its sentence once, with no explanation or moral, and doesn't end on "full stop".

**For your judgment:**
- **Length.** At about 265 words the chapter is well under its thirteen hundred, and the book is now about 6,500 words against the "about twelve thousand" in `AGENTS.md`. Short is the rule here, but you may want to change that target rather than leave a figure the book won't reach.

The lines are right and the order is right, and "Nobody noticed, including me" is mine now. But it's a list of endings, not a chapter yet. The last chapter needs one scene.

Here's the scene, and it's true. The first night I wrote this book, I ran the tool on it, the way I'd run it on Full Stop a thousand times. It found one problem. This book said "eleven chapters", and this book has nine, and the tool, which I had built for Full Stop, flagged Full Stop's own number as a mistake. I had to write the tool a note telling it that the count belonged to another book. It was the first time I had told the tool anything about Full Stop that wasn't a complaint.

Put it after "Then I started this one, which is how I found out," so the admission that the book was written with the tool comes out of it. The chapter can run to seven hundred words if the scene earns them. No padding beyond that.

Leave the twelve thousand in the guide alone for now. The blind read will tell us whether the book wants more, and I'd rather a reader decide that than either of us.

The wrapper splitting "Which one?" from "I said." is my tool's fault, not yours. Leave it.

content.text:
The scene is in, right after "Then I started this one, which is how I found out," and all five checks pass. The chapter is now 390 words. The scene didn't need more than that, so it stops well short of seven hundred. Nothing is committed.

**The scene:**

> The first night, I ran the tool on it, the way I had run it on Full Stop a thousand times.
> There wasn't much of it yet.
>
> It found one problem.
>
> It printed the sentence, with the chapter and the line, the way it always did.
> This book said "eleven chapters".
> This book has nine.
>
> The tool, which I had built for Full Stop, had flagged Full Stop's own number as a mistake.
>
> I looked at it for a while.
> Then I wrote the tool a note telling it that the count belonged to another book.
> It took one line.
>
> It was the first time I had told the tool anything about Full Stop that wasn't a complaint.
>
> I ran it again.
> Nothing.

"This book was written with the tool." follows straight after, so the admission comes out of the scene.

**Lines I invented**, to cut if they aren't true:
- "There wasn't much of it yet."
- "It printed the sentence, with the chapter and the line": this matches how The Demo describes the tool's output.
- "I looked at it for a while."
- "It took one line." The note in the sidecar is in fact one line.
- "I ran it again. Nothing."

**Other changes:**
- **Sidecar:** the length guidance now says at most about seven hundred words, only if the scene earns them. Two new guidance lines say where the scene goes and that the chapter is one scene, not a list of endings.
- **Spec:** `#written-with-the-tool` now holds the first night's run, the note, and that it was the first thing Cy told the tool about Full Stop that wasn't a complaint. I added a trail entry for your message.
- **`AGENTS.md`:** the twelve-thousand figure is unchanged. I added a note that it stays until the blind read says whether the book wants more, so a later assistant doesn't raise it again.
- **Wrapper:** the split between "Which one?" and "I said." is still there, as you asked.

This session now backs four trail entries and isn't captured yet, so run `quirework provenance ingest claude` when you close it.
